# Feature Fusion Foundry — Complete Feature Catalog

**868 capabilities**. Generated from the v1.3 registry.

## Storage & Local Data

### IndexedDB

**Summary:** Structured transactional browser database for application state.

IndexedDB is a distinct capability within Storage & Local Data. Structured transactional browser database for application state. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is durable state, portability and data ownership.

A production implementation should avoid coupling IndexedDB directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include offline-first applications, large datasets, portable knowledge commons, local AI assets. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

**Implementation:** Implementation pattern: schema versioning, transactional boundaries, quota behavior, recovery and explicit export paths. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for IndexedDB; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

**Example:** Store projects, tasks, evidence and preferences locally.

**Recommended use:** offline-first applications, large datasets, portable knowledge commons, local AI assets

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect IndexedDB through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

**Risks / failure modes:** Failure modes to design for include silent data loss, incompatible migrations, quota exhaustion and stale duplicate state. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

**Graceful fallback:** Graceful fallback: fall back to simpler browser storage or explicit file export while preserving readable core data. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

**Maturity:** stable

### RBAC

**Summary:** Role-based access control.

RBAC is a distinct capability within Identity, Authentication & Authorization. Role-based access control. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is identity assurance and scoped authorization.

A production implementation should avoid coupling RBAC directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include public communities, enterprise collaboration, moderated spaces, sensitive projects. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

**Implementation:** Implementation pattern: authentication separate from authorization, session expiry, revocation, recovery and object-level permission checks. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for RBAC; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

**Example:** Give reviewers approval rights and contributors edit rights.

**Recommended use:** public communities, enterprise collaboration, moderated spaces, sensitive projects

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect RBAC through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

**Risks / failure modes:** Failure modes to design for include account takeover, over-broad roles, orphaned sessions and irrecoverable identities. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

**Graceful fallback:** Graceful fallback: support guest/local mode or reduced privileges where authentication is unavailable. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

**Maturity:** stable

Source freshness is a distinct capability within Evidence, Provenance & Integrity. Record publication and retrieval dates. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is traceable claims and provenance.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Source freshness directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include research platforms, institutional decisions, public dashboards, AI synthesis. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

**Implementation:** Implementation pattern: stable identifiers, source metadata, review state, lineage, contradiction handling and exportability. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Source freshness; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

**Example:** Prompt a review when a source ages past its update interval.

**Recommended use:** research platforms, institutional decisions, public dashboards, AI synthesis

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect Source freshness through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

**Risks / failure modes:** Failure modes to design for include citation drift, stale sources, fabricated provenance and conflating opinion with evidence. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

**Graceful fallback:** Graceful fallback: show uncertainty explicitly and preserve source records even when advanced analysis is unavailable. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

**Maturity:** stable

**Summary:** Use locale-correct grammatical forms.

Pluralization is a distinct capability within Internationalization & Localization. Use locale-correct grammatical forms. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is internationalization & localization.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Pluralization directly to unrelated UI or transport code. **Implementation:** Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

**Example:** Render 1 task versus 2 tasks correctly across languages.

**Recommended use:** global communities, cross-border research, education, international institutions

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect Pluralization through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. Instance policy is a distinct capability within Federation & Multi-Instance Commons. Declare moderation, retention and federation rules. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is federation & multi-instance commons.

A production implementation should avoid coupling Instance policy directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include community-owned platforms, universities, municipal networks, global commons. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

**Implementation:** Implementation pattern: clear contracts, capability detection, versioning, observability and documented fallback behavior. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for Instance policy; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

**Example:** Let a community node refuse unwanted peers.

**Recommended use:** community-owned platforms, universities, municipal networks, global commons

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect Instance policy through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. **Example:** Use Geospatial search in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect Geospatial search through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. WASM media transcoding is a distinct capability within Media & Rich Collaboration. Transcode supported media locally when browser codecs or formats are insufficient. In this Foundry it is treated as a composable building block rather than a checkbox: the implementation should define what data it owns, which events or APIs it consumes and emits, what permissions it needs, how users can see its state, and what happens when it is unavailable. The primary architectural objective is rich audio, video and image collaboration.

A production implementation should avoid coupling WASM media transcoding directly to unrelated UI or transport code. Prefer a small adapter or service boundary, versioned inputs and outputs, feature detection where browser support varies, explicit initialization and cleanup, and observable error states. For online multiplayer systems, decide whether the capability is local-only, replicated peer state, authoritative server state, or derived/cache state. For AI-assisted systems, label whether generated material is advisory, draft, reviewed or verified before it can change consequential shared state.

Recommended contexts include remote meetings, field evidence, education, media-rich games. The feature should remain portable: project data should survive implementation replacement where practical, and a user should be able to understand why the feature exists, what it does, and what trade-offs it introduces.

**Implementation:** Implementation pattern: permission gating, local processing, codec support, file limits, captions and bandwidth adaptation. Start with a typed or schema-validated interface for WASM media transcoding; define initialization, cleanup, timeout/cancellation behavior, permissions and telemetry/privacy boundaries; then add tests for normal operation and failure. Keep UI state separate from durable domain state. If the capability participates in multiplayer, define ordering, idempotency, replay and reconnect behavior. If it processes external or user-supplied content, validate at the trust boundary and render untrusted content safely.

**Example:** Use WASM media transcoding in a real project only after defining its data boundaries, capability checks and fallback behavior.

**Recommended use:** remote meetings, field evidence, education, media-rich games

**Feature fusion:** Fusion guidance: connect WASM media transcoding through the shared route, capability, event and schema registries instead of calling other modules ad hoc. It normally gains value when paired with persistence, provenance, accessibility, diagnostics and an explicit fallback. In a feature-fusion prompt, ask the coding model to name the events shared with adjacent modules, the source of truth for each piece of state, and the condition under which this feature should deactivate or downgrade.

**Risks / failure modes:** Failure modes to design for include privacy leakage, huge files, unsupported codecs and inaccessible media. Also test unsupported browsers, interrupted initialization, stale versions, malformed inputs, permission denial, offline transitions and partial upgrades. Do not present availability, security, correctness or impact claims as proven unless the relevant checks were actually performed.

**Graceful fallback:** Graceful fallback: provide text/transcript/static-image alternatives and conventional file upload/download. Preserve readable/exportable state whenever possible, explain the degraded mode in plain language, and never make an optional advanced capability a single point of failure for the whole workspace.

**Maturity:** stable
